The Jupyter Kernel API does not expose server IDs or connection URLs.

Detecting durable kernel usage from the public API alone is unreliable. Checking for any active kernel would incorrectly suppress the selection button for local kernels. Tracking via notebook metadata appears more practical.

Remote kernels often leave markers. Notebook document metadata could reveal session associations. The user's instruction is ambiguous. It may refer to durable kernel selection or any kernel selection.

The user's wording points toward a durable-specific transition. The button should appear when no durable kernel is active, then swap for a compact status indicator once a durable kernel is selected. Because the public API cannot reliably confirm the notebook uses the durable server, heuristic checks will be needed.

Heuristic checks are being weighed: verifying notebook metadata against the durable server URL, or tracking notebook URIs that completed the selection flow. The preferred outcome is replacing the button with a compact state indicator rather than hiding it entirely. A concrete implementation plan is being drafted.

The button will move to the status group beside the kernel picker. A toggle pattern will switch between a selection command and a compact status menu based on a context key. That key will rely on the durable server being registered and the active notebook having a kernel, though local kernels would also satisfy that check. Inspecting notebook metadata is a lighter way to distinguish durable connections.

A refined heuristic is being considered: show the selection button until the external kernel is running and the user has actually chosen from the durable collection. The notebook's `kernelspec` metadata and the VS Code notebook API's `selectKernel` method are being examined to identify the selected kernel controller.

A dedicated context key, `jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.activeForNotebook`, is being introduced to cleanly signal when a durable kernel is active for the current notebook.

A simpler rule is emerging: always show the compact status button when the durable server is running, and only show the Select button when no durable server is available or no kernel is attached to the notebook. This avoids fragile metadata checks because remote server associations live in VS Code's memento rather than the notebook file itself.

The previous simple rule is rejected because it would still show the Select button when a durable server is running alongside a local kernel. Two toolbar entries with distinct when clauses are now preferred: Select when the notebook is not on a durable kernel, and a compact icon-only Status when it is. The durable flag will be detected by polling the active editor and checking for a kernel plus server association.

Querying the Jupyter server's `/api/sessions` endpoint could reliably detect whether a notebook is actively using the durable kernel by matching session paths. This aligns with existing health-probing infrastructure. For a first version, however, relying on `getKernel` presence combined with a running durable server is sufficient. The goal is polished UX, not perfect attribution.

The sessions API check is now the chosen approach because it is more accurate and DurableServerManager already performs HTTP probes. Existing notebook type and context keys are being checked as a simpler alternative. For the compact toolbar button, the existing `statusMenu` command will be contributed with an icon such as `$(server-environment)` and a short title like `:8888` or `Durable`. The `shortTitle` field in the command contribution will keep the label minimal.

Command titles in package.json are static, so dynamic state like `:8888 idle` cannot be shown directly. Changing the title via `setContext` or `executeCommand` does not update the menu label. Tooltips are also static. A StatusBarItem in the notebook toolbar is not possible. The compact button will likely use an empty or minimal title paired with a tooltip to display runtime details.

The compact status button will open the existing `statusMenu` command. It will use a static title such as "Durable Jupyter" and rely on the status bar for runtime state. This avoids the limitation of static command titles in package.json.

The compact toolbar button will likely be purely icon-based, opening the status menu. The port number is dynamic, so a static title remains impossible. Multiple commands with different titles were considered, but the port still cannot be shown.

The Select button will move to the `status` group at the far right, directly beside the kernel picker. When a durable kernel is active, it will be hidden and replaced by a compact icon-only `statusMenu` button with a short title. Clicking it will open the same QuickPick as the status bar. The existing status bar will remain for full dynamic state. A context key updated by the status monitor will drive the visibility toggle.

A simpler interpretation is emerging: the Select Durable Kernel button might only need to hide once any kernel is selected, since the default kernel picker already displays the active kernel. This would treat the button as an onboarding shortcut rather than a durable-specific control.

The simpler reading is confirmed: the Select button should disappear once any kernel is active, since the default kernel picker already displays the selected kernel. The compact durable status button is treated as an optional enhancement rather than a mandatory replacement. The visibility toggle will rely on a context key derived from `getKernel`.

The toolbar layout is now fully defined. The Select button appears only when no kernel is active. Once any kernel is selected, it hides and is replaced by a compact durable status button when a durable server is running. If a kernel is active but no durable server is present, the toolbar remains empty. An alternative is also being considered: showing the durable status button whenever a durable server exists, even without an active kernel.

The compact button will use a static title such as "Durable" with the `$(server-environment)` icon. Its menu order is set to `@-9` so it sorts directly after the kernel picker at `-10`, placing it at the far right of the status group. A brief flash of the Select button before a kernel starts is acceptable.

VS Code toolbar commands support `shortTitle` for compact labels. The status command will gain an icon for toolbar visibility. The exact when clauses are now defined: `selectKernel` appears when a Jupyter notebook has no durable kernel, while `statusInToolbar` appears when a durable kernel is active and running.

  "plan": "# Durable Kernel Toolbar Placement\n\n## Problem\n\n[`package.json`](package.json) currently contributes Select Durable Kernel on the **left** execute strip:\n\n```1138:1142:package.json\n{\n  \"command\": \"jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.selectKernel\",\n  \"group\": \"navigation/execute@10\",\n  \"when\": \"notebookType == jupyter-notebook \u0026\u0026 config.jupyter-cell-tags.features.durableKernel\"\n}\n```\n\nVS Code’s notebook global toolbar renders `navigation*` groups on the left and `status*` on the right. The built-in kernel picker uses `group: 'status'` (order `-10`), so our button never sits next to it. Nothing hides or replaces the button after a kernel is attached.\n\n## Approach\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  subgraph rightToolbar [Notebook toolbar right]\n    KernelPicker[Built-in kernel picker]\n    OurBtn[Select or Compact Durable]\n  end\n  HasKernel{notebookHasKernel?}\n  Running{durable server running?}\n  HasKernel --\u003e|no| Select[Select Durable Kernel]\n  HasKernel --\u003e|yes| Running\n  Running --\u003e|yes| Compact[Compact Durable icon]\n  Running --\u003e|no| Hidden[Hide our toolbar item]\n  Compact --\u003e|click| StatusMenu[statusMenu QuickPick]\n  Select --\u003e|click| SelectKernel[selectKernel command]\n```\n\n**Chosen UX (locked):**\n1. Place our control in `status` next to the kernel picker (far right).\n2. Before a kernel is attached → show **Select Durable Kernel…**.\n3. After a kernel is attached and a durable server is registered → replace with a **compact** toolbar button (icon + short title) that runs `statusMenu` (same QuickPick as the status bar).\n4. After a kernel is attached but no durable server → show nothing from us (built-in kernel picker is enough).\n5. Keep the existing bottom status bar as-is for the full dynamic label (`Durable :port idle`).\n\nDetection uses Jupyter’s `kernels.getKernel(uri)` (already used in [`statusMonitor.ts`](src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts)): a non-undefined kernel means “a kernel has been selected/started” for the active notebook. Perfect “this is *our* durable session” attribution is not exposed by the public Jupyter API; pairing `notebookHasKernel` with `externalKernel.running` is the practical signal for when to show the compact Durable control.\n\n## Changes\n\n### 1. `package.json` — toolbar + compact command presentation\n\n- Move Select contribution from `navigation/execute@10` to **`status@-9`** (kernel picker is `status` order `-10`; `-9` places us immediately beside it on the right).\n- When for Select:\n  - `notebookType == jupyter-notebook \u0026\u0026 config.jupyter-cell-tags.features.durableKernel \u0026\u0026 !jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.notebookHasKernel`\n- Add toolbar entry for `jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.statusMenu`:\n  - `group`: `status@-9`\n  - `when`: notebook + feature + `jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.notebookHasKernel \u0026\u0026 jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.running`\n- Give `statusMenu` an **icon** (e.g. `$(server-environment)`) and a short **title** / `shortTitle` such as `Durable` so the toolbar control stays narrow (labels still depend on `notebook.globalToolbarShowLabel`).\n\n### 2. [`src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts`](src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts) — context key\n\nIn `refresh()` (already polls health and resolves kernel status):\n\n- Set `jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.notebookHasKernel` via `setContext` to whether `getKernel(activeNotebook.uri)` returned a kernel.\n- Clear it when there is no active notebook editor.\n- Reuse the existing kernel listener path so busy/idle changes keep the context accurate after attach/detach.\n\n`jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.running` is already maintained in [`DurableServerManager.syncContextKeys()`](src/externalKernel/DurableServerManager.ts).\n\n### 3. No handler rewrites required\n\n[`startup.ts`](src/externalKernel/startup.ts) already registers `selectKernel` and `statusMenu`. Toolbar only needs the contribution + when-clause toggle (same pattern as notebook filter set/clear at `@9`).\n\n## Manual check\n\n- Open a Jupyter notebook with durableKernel enabled: Select appears on the **right**, next to Select Kernel.\n- Select a kernel (durable or otherwise): Select disappears.\n- With a durable server registered and a kernel attached: compact **Durable** control appears in the same spot; click opens the status QuickPick.\n- Switch to a notebook with no kernel: Select returns.",

The `actionProvider` returns a `NotebooKernelActionViewItem` for `SELECT_KERNEL_ID`, but otherwise falls back to `ActionViewWithLabel`. That fallback path may be suppressing the button.

The fallback path searches `this._primaryActions`, which only contains left-toolbar actions. Because the status action is not in that list, the lookup returns undefined and the button is suppressed.

_**Agent (default)**_

The button was hidden by a when-clause gap: once any kernel was attached, Select disappeared, but the compact Durable control only appears when a durable server is also running — so with a normal kernel and no durable server, nothing showed.

**Fix:** Select now shows whenever the compact control does not (no kernel **or** no durable server). Compact Durable still replaces it only when both a kernel is attached and a durable server is registered.

Reload the extension host and check the far right of the notebook toolbar (next to Select Kernel).

---

_**User**_

the button is there, but it's very hard to see! When durable kernel is in-use it should have a green indicator or color, and when it's not active it should have a red border or something equally distinct

---

_**Agent (default)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The durable kernel toolbar button needs clear visual feedback. Green indicates active use. A red border or similar distinct color shows inactive status.

VS Code toolbar buttons likely cannot support custom borders or colors directly. Using different icons for each state may be more practical. The status bar already handles dynamic icons and text well.

Package.json toolbar icons cannot carry custom colors. Programmatic swapping via when clauses is another option. Severity-themed icons like $(pass-filled) and $(error) could indicate active versus inactive states.

Custom SVG icons with baked-in green and red colors are another viable option. Each state can have its own light and dark variant. This avoids relying on theme colors or programmatic swapping.

Specific built-in icons were considered but rejected because they do not provide the requested green indicator or red border. The plan is to use two custom SVG icons: green for active use and red for inactive. These will be assigned to the existing selectKernel and statusMenu commands. Status bar colors may also be updated for consistency.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
VS Code UX guidelines prohibit adding custom colors for editor actions. This constraint complicates the request for a green indicator when durable kernel is active and a red border when inactive.

Status bar items support ThemeColor for background and foreground, which could provide the requested green and red indicators without violating the guideline. Custom SVG icons with baked-in colors are another option, though they may fight the current theme.

Codicons such as `$(pass-filled)` or `$(error)` might indicate state, but they do not guarantee green or red colors on the toolbar. Tree views support ThemeIcon colors, yet package.json commands cannot set them. A better approach for toolbar visibility is now being considered.

Custom SVG icons with explicit green fill for active state and red stroke for inactive state are the chosen approach. Saturated colors should work across light and dark themes without separate variants. The status bar will also use warning or error backgrounds to match the toolbar state. Currently, compact mode indicates durable kernel is active, while select mode indicates it is inactive.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
VS Code toolbar icons cannot use CSS borders or theme colors. Custom SVGs with baked-in green and red will make the durable kernel button clearly distinguishable.

The status bar will mirror the toolbar colors. Green indicates the durable kernel is in use. Red indicates it is inactive. The SVGs will be 16 by 16 pixels with one pixel of padding.

Green fills the active glyph. A red stroke frames the inactive outline. Fixed colors override VS Code’s single-color icon guideline because blending would hide the state. The new icons must be packed into the extension bundle and verified against .vscodeignore.

Two SVG files will be added under `media/`: `durable-kernel-active.svg` and `durable-kernel-inactive.svg`. They will be wired into the status menu and select kernel commands in `package.json`. The status bar will switch to `statusBarItem.warningBackground` and `warningForeground` when the kernel is down.

{
  "name": "Durable Button Visibility",
  "overview": "Make the durable-kernel notebook toolbar control visually unmistakable by swapping in custom green (in-use) and red-bordered (inactive) SVG icons, and mirror that state on the status bar with theme colors.",
  "plan": "# Durable Kernel Button Visibility\n\n## Constraint\n\nNotebook toolbar buttons from `package.json` cannot use CSS borders or `ThemeColor`. The reliable way to get a **green / red** look is **custom SVG command icons** (fixed colors that stay visible on both light and dark toolbars).\n\nExisting toggle already maps to the two states we care about in [`package.json`](package.json):\n\n| State | Command | Current icon |\n|-------|---------|--------------|\n| Not active | `selectKernel` | `$(vm)` (low contrast) |\n| In use | `statusMenu` | `$(server-environment)` (low contrast) |\n\n## Approach\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  Inactive[Select command] --\u003e|red border SVG| Toolbar\n  Active[statusMenu command] --\u003e|green SVG| Toolbar\n  Monitor[statusMonitor.refresh] --\u003e|ThemeColor| StatusBar\n```\n\n### 1. Add icons under `media/`\n\nCreate two 16×16 SVGs (1px padding, centered):\n\n- [`media/durable-kernel-inactive.svg`](media/durable-kernel-inactive.svg) — compact server/vm glyph inside a **red rounded-rect stroke** (`#e11d48` or similar) so “not active” reads as a bordered control.\n- [`media/durable-kernel-active.svg`](media/durable-kernel-active.svg) — same glyph with a **green filled badge/dot or green stroke+fill** (`#16a34a`) so “in use” is obvious at a glance.\n\nUse the same asset for light and dark paths (saturated traffic-light colors read on both).\n\n### 2. Wire icons in [`package.json`](package.json)\n\n```json\n\"jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.selectKernel\": {\n  \"icon\": {\n    \"light\": \"media/durable-kernel-inactive.svg\",\n    \"dark\": \"media/durable-kernel-inactive.svg\"\n  }\n},\n\"jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.statusMenu\": {\n  \"icon\": {\n    \"light\": \"media/durable-kernel-active.svg\",\n    \"dark\": \"media/durable-kernel-active.svg\"\n  }\n}\n```\n\nNo when-clause changes; the existing Select ↔ Durable swap already drives which icon appears.\n\n### 3. Mirror state on the status bar in [`src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts`](src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts)\n\nIn `refresh()`, after computing health / kernel attachment:\n\n- Durable server present and health `up` → `statusBar.color = new ThemeColor('charts.green')`, clear `backgroundColor`.\n- Health `down` or unknown → `statusBar.color = new ThemeColor('errorForeground')` and `backgroundColor = new ThemeColor('statusBarItem.errorBackground')` (cleared when healthy again).\n\nThis reinforces the same green/red language next to the toolbar without depending on SVG packing for the status bar.\n\n### 4. Packaging\n\nConfirm `media/**` is not excluded by [`.vscodeignore`](.vscodeignore) (add an allow rule only if needed) so the VSIX/debug host can load the icons.\n\n## Manual check\n\n- No durable / not in-use: right toolbar shows Select with **red-bordered** icon.\n- Durable running + kernel attached: icon swaps to **green** Durable control.\n- Status bar text tint follows green when healthy, error styling when down.\n",

The red icon appears correctly on the Select Durable Kernel button. After connecting successfully, the toolbar icon remains red and never turns green. The status bar text updates properly, but the icon state does not.

The status bar turns green once the durable server is healthy, independent of `notebookHasKernel`. The toolbar icon needs both `notebookHasKernel` and `running` to be true. Jupyter's `getKernel` only returns kernels that have already been started by the user. A durable kernel may register without being started, so `getKernel` does not return it until a cell is executed. This explains why the status bar shows green while the toolbar icon stays red.

Remote durable kernels might never appear in `getKernel`, or `notebookHasKernel` might fail to update after selection. The Select icon remains active because its when clause is still true. A better signal for an active durable connection is needed.

The `running` context key is likely correct, since the status bar already shows green. The problem is isolated to `notebookHasKernel` remaining false. One fix would be to remove the `notebookHasKernel` requirement for the green toolbar icon and instead rely on `running` and health status.

Three specific fixes are under consideration. A new `durableActive` context key could combine `running` and healthy status to drive the icon swap. Alternatively, the green icon could simply depend on `externalKernel.running` alone, dropping the `notebookHasKernel` check entirely. The user's original intent was to hide the Select button once a durable kernel is chosen and display a green status indicator while the kernel is actively in use.

Polling more aggressively after the selectKernel command may help detect the kernel state faster. The toolbar icon should align with the status bar signal rather than relying solely on notebookHasKernel.

A simple `running && healthy` rule would always show the green icon whenever the durable server is up, even if no notebook is connected to it. That misses the intended behavior of hiding the Select button once a kernel is chosen. If `getKernel` cannot detect durable remote kernels, querying `/api/sessions` on the durable server for the current notebook path may provide a better signal.
</details></think>
